title: The Servant Who Listens and Does Not Turn Back
summary: God answers the exiles' complaint that he has divorced them or sold them off: their own sins sent them away, and his hand is not too short to bring them back. Then a new voice speaks, the Servant, who is taught by God morning by morning, submits to beating and spitting without turning back, and trusts God to vindicate him. The chapter closes by calling those who fear the LORD to trust him in the dark, and warning those who light their own fires.
story: Chapter 49 ended with Zion saying the LORD had forsaken her and with God insisting he could not forget her. Chapter 50 presses the same question from a different angle, in the language of divorce and debt. Then, for the second time in two chapters, the Servant speaks for himself. In the first two Servant passages (42:1-9 and 49:1-6) the Servant was chosen, gentle, and called to bring light to the nations; here, for the first time, his calling brings him suffering. That turn prepares directly for the fourth and fullest portrait of the Servant in 52:13 to 53:12, where his suffering becomes the means by which others are healed.
historical:
The chapter addresses Israelites who feel abandoned by God. On the reading held by most scholars, that means Judeans in Babylon in the mid-sixth century BC, a generation or two after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC; on the traditional view that Isaiah wrote the whole book, it is the eighth-century prophet speaking ahead to that exile (see the introduction). Either way, the audience's question is real. Their city was in ruins, their temple gone, and their families scattered. To many it looked as though their God had either been defeated by Babylon's gods or had simply given them up.

The Servant's suffering in verses 5 to 9 has no named historical setting. Readers have long noticed its closeness to the experience of prophets like Jeremiah, who was beaten, put in stocks, and thrown into a cistern for speaking God's word (Jeremiah 20:2; 38:6). Whether the passage describes the prophet's own treatment, the faithful within Israel, or a figure still to come is discussed in the note on chapter 53.
cultural:
Two institutions of ordinary life stand behind verse 1. Under Deuteronomy 24:1-4 a husband who divorced his wife gave her a written certificate, which freed her to remarry and, once she had, barred him from taking her back. And a man overwhelmed by debt could sell his children into servitude to pay his creditors (compare 2 Kings 4:1, where a creditor comes to take a widow's sons). God asks where the certificate is and which creditor he owes. There is none. He did not formally divorce Zion, and he is in debt to no one. The exile happened because of Israel's sins, not because God's hands were tied, and so nothing stands in the way of his taking his people back.

The insults of verse 6 carried heavy weight in that world. Striking a man on the back was a punishment for fools and wrongdoers (Proverbs 10:13). Pulling out a man's beard was a deliberate humiliation of his manhood and standing; when an Ammonite king shaved half the beards of David's envoys, it was treated as an act of war (2 Samuel 10:4-6). Spitting in someone's face was a public mark of contempt (Deuteronomy 25:9). The Servant accepts all three without retaliating.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 3 are a disputation, a form Isaiah uses often, in which God quotes or implies his hearers' objection and answers it with pointed questions. Verses 4 to 9 are the third of the four passages called the Servant Songs, spoken in the first person. It moves in steps: the Servant is given a trained tongue and an open ear (4-5), he submits to abuse (6), and he stakes everything on God's help, using the language of a lawsuit (7-9). The phrase “the Lord GOD” (Hebrew Adonai YHWH) opens four of its lines like a refrain. Verses 10 and 11 apply the song to the listeners and set two paths side by side: walking in darkness while trusting God, or walking by the light of a fire you kindled yourself.

outline.t: No certificate of divorce, no creditor: the LORD can still save
The Servant taught morning by morning
The Servant beaten, unashamed, and sure of vindication
Trusting God in the dark, or walking by your own fire

doctrines.note: “You were sold for your iniquities” (verse 1). The exile is not arbitrary and it is not God's weakness. Israel's own transgressions sent them away, and the chapter insists on this precisely so that the promise of return can be believed.

The Servant suffers not because he has rebelled but because he has listened. The chapter separates suffering from guilt: faithfulness to God's word can lead straight into disgrace, and God's help does not always mean escape from pain but vindication through it.

Verse 10 describes a believer who fears the LORD yet has no light, and tells him to lean on his God anyway. Trust in Scripture is not the absence of darkness but the refusal to manufacture a false light in it.

words.note: Limmud, one who is taught, a disciple. The Servant has “the tongue of discipleship” and listens “as a disciple” (verse 4). The same word describes the prophet's followers in 8:16 and the children of Zion who will all be taught by the LORD in 54:13. The Servant's power to sustain the weary comes from first being a learner himself.

Challamish, flint, the hardest common stone in Israel's hills. The Servant sets his face “like flint” (verse 7), not in stubborn pride but in settled resolve. Ezekiel 3:8-9 uses similar language for the hardened forehead God gives his prophet to face a resistant people.

Tsadaq, to be in the right, or in its causative form to declare or prove someone in the right. “The One who vindicates Me is near” (verse 8) is courtroom language: the Servant's accusers may beat him, but the judge is on his side. The same verb returns in 53:11, where the righteous Servant will justify many.

christ: The Gospels describe Jesus receiving exactly the treatment of verse 6: he was spat on, struck, and mocked before the high priest's council and by the Roman soldiers (Matthew 26:67; Mark 15:19). Luke says that when the time for his death drew near, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), a phrase many readers connect with the face set like flint. Paul echoes verses 8 and 9 in Romans 8:33-34, where he asks who can bring a charge against God's chosen ones or condemn them, since God is the one who justifies and Christ has died and been raised. The New Testament does not quote this song directly as a prediction, as it does chapter 53, but it draws on its picture of a Servant who listens, suffers, and is vindicated.

hard.q: Is God saying he did divorce Israel, or that he didn't?
hard.a: Verse 1 can seem to contradict other passages. Jeremiah 3:8 says God gave faithless Israel (the northern kingdom) a certificate of divorce, and Hosea's marriage enacted God's broken covenant. Isaiah 50:1 asks where Zion's certificate is, implying there isn't one. Most interpreters see no real contradiction, because the two prophets are making different points with the same image. Jeremiah uses divorce to show how serious the breach was. Isaiah's question uses the legal detail of Deuteronomy 24, under which a completed divorce made return impossible, to insist that God never made the separation final. The mother was sent away, but not with papers that would bar her return. Read this way, the verse is not denying the seriousness of the exile but denying that it was the last word.

questions: The Servant is taught “morning by morning” before he speaks to the weary. What would it look like for your words to others to come out of listening first?
Verse 10 imagines someone who fears God but walks in darkness with no light. Have you known that kind of season, and what helped or did not help?
What are the fires people kindle for themselves when God seems silent, and why does the chapter treat them as dangerous?
